content: Micrococcus is a genus of bacteria belonging to the family Micrococcaceae. These bacteria are found in diverse environments, including human skin, water, dust, and soil. The cells of Micrococcus are Gram-positive, spherical in shape, and range in size from approximately 0.5 to 3 micrometers in diameter. They typically appear in tetrads. The cell wall of Micrococcus is notably thick, constituting up to 50% of the cell's mass. The genome of Micrococcus is characterized by a high guanine and cytosine (GC) content, typically ranging from 65% to 75%. Additionally, Micrococcus species often harbor plasmids, which can vary in size from 1 to 100 megadaltons (MDa) and confer advantageous traits to the organism. Certain species of Micrococcus, such as Micrococcus luteus and Micrococcus roseus, produce distinctively colored colonies—yellow and pink, respectively—when cultured on solid media. Notably, isolates of M. luteus have been observed to overproduce riboflavin when grown in the presence of toxic organic pollutants like pyridine. However, hybridization studies have revealed that species within the Micrococcus genus exhibit low genetic similarity, with as little as 50% sequence homology. This finding suggests that some species currently classified under Micrococcus may eventually be reassigned to other microbial genera based on ribosomal RNA analysis. Micrococci are widely distributed in the environment and have been isolated from human skin, animal-derived products, dairy products, and beer. They are also found in water, dust, and soil. On human skin, M. luteus is known to metabolize compounds in sweat, producing substances that contribute to unpleasant odors. These bacteria are capable of thriving in environments with low water availability or high salt concentrations. While most Micrococcus species are mesophilic, some, such as Micrococcus antarcticus, are psychrophilic and adapted to cold environments like Antarctica. Although Micrococcus does not form spores, its cells can survive for extended periods under adverse conditions. For instance, unprotected soil micrococci cultures have been successfully revived after 10 years of refrigeration. Remarkably, research by Greenblat et al. has demonstrated that M. luteus has survived for at least 34,000 to 170,000 years, as evidenced by 16S rRNA analysis, and possibly even longer. Micrococcus is generally considered a saprophytic or commensal organism, but it can act as an opportunistic pathogen, particularly in individuals with compromised immune systems, such as those with HIV. Identifying Micrococcus as the causative agent of an infection can be challenging because it is a normal component of the skin microbiota and is rarely associated with disease. However, in rare cases, pulmonary infections caused by Micrococcus have resulted in fatalities among immunocompromised patients. Other infections linked to Micrococcus include recurrent bacteremia, septic shock, septic arthritis, endocarditis, meningitis, and cavitating pneumonia, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals. Micrococcus species exhibit significant metabolic versatility, enabling them to utilize a wide range of unusual substrates, including pyridine, herbicides, chlorinated biphenyls, and oil. This metabolic capability suggests that Micrococcus plays a role in the detoxification or biodegradation of various environmental pollutants. Additionally, some Micrococcus isolates are known to produce valuable compounds, such as long-chain aliphatic hydrocarbons (C21-C34), which are used in the production of lubricating oils.
